src: APPSC Group-I Prelims Paper-I Screening Test 2024
s:
In connection with the veto power of the Indian President, which one of the following statement/statements is/are valid?

I. The Indian President possesses 'Suspensive Veto' in the case of Money Bills but not in the case of Finance Bills.

II. The Indian President can exercise 'Absolute Veto' with respect to the Government Bills at all times.

III. The Indian President enjoys 'Pocket Veto' indefinitely whereas the American President possesses 'Qualified Veto'.

IV. The objective of the veto power in being conferred upon the Indian President is to ensure a system of checks and balances between the office of the President and that of the power of the Parliament.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
Under which Article of the Indian Constitution, the President of India enjoys the power to withhold his assent to any Bill passed by both the Houses of the Parliament?
x: According to Article 111 of the Indian Constitution, when a Bill has been passed by both the Houses of Parliament, it shall be presented to the President and the President shall declare that either he assents to the Bill or that he withholds assent therefrom.

s: In pocket veto, the President of India can keep a bill for how much duration?
x: In a pocket veto the President neither assents, rejects nor returns the Bill, and Art. 111 prescribes no time limit, so he can hold it for an indefinite period.

s: Does the President of India have veto power?
o: The constitution is silent on this
x: The Indian President has absolute, suspensive and pocket vetoes, so the answer is Yes; he lacks only the qualified veto.

s: Which of the following is a " pocket veto " power in the Indian context?
o: Speaker of Lok Sabha not allowing presentation of a bill
President keeping a bill pendin, with him, without any time limit and without approving
Prime Minister removing ministers from his Cabinet without any reason
Rajya Sabha vetoing the provisions of a bill approved by Lok Sabha
x: A pocket veto is the President's practice of keeping a bill pending indefinitely, because Article 111 sets no time limit, without assenting to it or returning it.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the pocket veto of the President of India?
o: As in the USA, the President must decide within 10 days, failing which the Bill becomes law.
It is possible because Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the President's decision on a Bill.
Under it, the President neither assents to, nor rejects, nor returns the Bill.
President Giani Zail Singh used it on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.
x: The 10-day limit is a US feature; Article 111 sets no time limit in India, which is what makes the pocket veto possible.

s: To which Bills does the suspensive veto of the President apply?
x: The suspensive veto (return once) applies only to Ordinary Bills, not Money Bills.

s: To which Bills is the absolute veto of the President usually applied?
x: The absolute veto is used for private members' Bills and for Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent.

s: Where is the rule that a Bill becomes law if not decided within 10 days found?
x: The 10-day rule is a US feature; Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the Indian President.

src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
s: All legislative proposals are brought before the Parliament in the form of:
What can the President do with a Money Bill passed by Parliament?
o: Assent or withhold assent, but not return it
Keep it pending only for ten days
x: For a Money Bill the President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration.

s: Which Amendment made the President's assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill mandatory?
x: The 24th Amendment, 1971 made assent mandatory; the President cannot reject or return such a Bill.

s: Which of the following Bills can the President NOT return for reconsideration?
x: Assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill is mandatory, so it cannot be returned; the one-time return power can apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II.

s: To Financial Bills of which category can the President's one-time power to return a Bill apply?
x: The one-time return power can apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II; Money Bills cannot be returned.

s: Among the following presidents of India, who was also the Secretary General of Non-Aligned Movement for some period?

Under which Article of the Indian Constitution did the President give his assent to the ordinance on electoral reforms when it was sent back to him by the Union Cabinet without making any changes (in the year 2002)?
x: Article 123 of the Constitution expressly vests the power to promulgate ordinances, and to give assent to them, in the President of India.

s: Who of the following presidents of India refused to give his assent to the Indian Post Office Bill?
x: President Gyani Zail Singh famously exercised a pocket veto by withholding his assent to the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill passed by Parliament. This incident is remembered as a notable instance of presidential assertion during his tenure.

s: Who among the following Presidents exercised a power which is ‘Pocket veto’ in Constitutional terminology?
x: A Pocket Veto is a legislative manoeuvre that allows a president to exercise that power over a Bill by taking no action (instead of affirmatively voting it or sending it back for reconsideration). To date, ‘Pocket Veto’ has been exercised only once in India by the President Gyani Zail Singh in 1986 on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.

s: The only instance when the President of India exercised his power of veto, is related to-
x: President Dr. Rajendra Prasad applied an absolute Veto on the advice of the Council of Ministers over the PEPSU Appropriation Bill 1954, Whereas President Gyani Zail Singh exercised the pocket veto in the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill in 1986. Hence, a pocket veto can be regarded as the veto power used by the President at his discretion. In Contrast, absolute veto is subject to the discretion of the Union Council of Ministers. Therefore, option (c) is the correct answer.

s: Who among the following, while serving as President, refused to sign the Indian Post Office Bill?
On which Bill did Dr. Rajendra Prasad exercise the absolute veto?
x: Rajendra Prasad used the absolute veto on the PEPSU Appropriation Bill, 1954, on the Council of Ministers' advice.

s: Which Bill did President Giani Zail Singh keep pending by using the pocket veto?
x: Zail Singh used the pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986, the only use at the Union level.

s: Identify the wrong statement with regard to Veto Power of the President of India.
o: He cannot return a Money Bill passed by the Parliament.
He has no Veto Power over Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368.
He has no Veto Power over an Ordinary Bill passed for second time by the Parliament.
He cannot Veto a Money Bill passed by the State Legislature duly forwarded by the Governor of a State.

s: Under which Article did the Supreme Court hold in 2025 that a Governor's indefinite inaction on a Bill is justiciable?
x: Indefinite inaction under Article 200 is justiciable, so the Governor has no presidential-style pocket veto.

s: Under which Article does the President declare or withhold assent to a State Bill reserved by the Governor?
x: Article 201 governs reserved State Bills; Article 200 is the Governor's own options.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold about courts in the November 2025 Presidential reference under Article 143?
o: Can fix a three-month timeline for assent
Can declare pending Bills deemed assented
Can direct the President to assent to any Bill
Cannot fix timelines for the Governor or the President
x: The five-judge bench held courts cannot fix timelines and there is no deemed assent, though the powers cannot be used arbitrarily.

s: In State of Tamil Nadu v Governor (8 April 2025), how many Tamil Nadu Bills were deemed assented?
x: The April 2025 ruling held indefinite inaction under Article 200 justiciable and deemed ten TN Bills assented.

s: Which of the following powers does the Governor NOT have over State Bills?
o: Reserving a Bill for the President
x: Under Article 200 the Governor may assent, withhold, return or reserve a Bill, but has no pocket veto.

s:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. An Ordinance can amend any Central Act.
II. An Ordinance can abridge a Fundamental Right.
III. An Ordinance can come into effect from a back date.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: An ordinance has the force of law under Article 13, so it cannot abridge a Fundamental Right, but it can amend Central Acts and operate retrospectively, so I and III are correct.

s: Who among the following has the power to promulgate ordinances under Article 123 of the Constitution of India?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
x: Art. 123 empowers the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session; the Speaker, Chairman and Attorney-General have no such power.

s: Under which of the following Articles of the Constitution, the President of India has been empowered to promulgate an ordinance?
x: Art. 123 is the ordinance-making provision for the President. Art. 360 deals with financial emergency, Art. 200 with the Governor's assent to Bills and Art. 356 with President's Rule.

s: The ordinance-making power of the President under Article 123 is regarded as a relic of which earlier enactment?
x: The President's ordinance-making power under Article 123 is a relic of the Government of India Act, 1935, which gave the Governor-General power to issue ordinances. The 1909 Act brought Morley-Minto reforms, the 1919 Act introduced dyarchy, and the 1947 Act ended British rule; none is the stated source of Article 123.

s: When can an ordinance be promulgated?
o: a Proclamation of Emergency is in force
the Lok Sabha passes a resolution permitting it
both Houses are in full session
x: An ordinance can be issued only when the legislature is in recess and the Head of State is satisfied that immediate action is needed; none can be issued while both Houses are sitting.

s: An ordinance has the same force, effect and limitations as which of the following?
o: An Act of Parliament or State Legislature
A judicial decree of the Supreme Court
An executive or administrative order only
x: An ordinance has the same force, effect and limits as an Act of Parliament or the State Legislature. It is legislative, not executive, and cannot amend the Constitution.

s: Which of this is the legislative power of the President according to constitution?
o: To summon the session of Parliament
To prorogate the session of Parliament
To adjourn the meeting of Parliament
x: The President is an integral part of the Parliament of India. He can promulgate ordinances when the Parliament is not in session. Thus ordinances must be approved by the Parliament within six weeks of its reassembly. He can also withdraw an ordinance at any time. The power to promulgate an ordinance, is thus the legislative power of the President. The Power of the President to promulgate ordinances is mentioned in Article 123 of the Constitution of India.

s: Under which Article is an ordinance treated as 'law', so that it is void if it abridges Fundamental Rights?
x: An ordinance is 'law' under Article 13(2) and is void if it abridges Fundamental Rights, though it can make or change tax provisions within legislative power.

s: Which of the following can an ordinance NOT do?
x: Within legislative competence an ordinance can amend Acts, act retrospectively and change taxes, but it cannot amend the Constitution.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ordinances?
o: The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time.
The ordinance-making power is beyond judicial review.
Re-promulgation without legislative ratification may subvert the Constitution.
The Governor can withdraw an ordinance at any time.
x: Ordinances are subject to judicial review; the other three statements are correct.

s: When can the President withdraw an ordinance?
o: Only within six weeks of reassembly
x: The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time; saying he cannot is a common trap.

s: Any Ordinance shall be approved by the parliament before the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of parliament. How the time shall be counted when the houses of Parliament reassemble on different days
o: The period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the date of assembly of the house whichever assembles
The period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the date of assembly of the house whichever assembles later
To approve Ordinance both Houses shall assemble on same date
This issue is left to the discretion of Lok sabha speaker

s: In India executive have the power to legislate by Ordinances. But Legislature shall approve it otherwise the ordinance can exist at most
x: The maximum gap between sessions is six months and the ordinance lapses six weeks after reassembly, so its maximum life is six months plus six weeks.

s: A Presidential Ordinance can remain in force
Which of the following statements is not correct regarding the issuance of Ordinance by the President?
o: It is linked to the legislative powers of Parliament
It ceases to exist after six weeks of Parliament Session
x: The President of India has been given the Power to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament under Article 123 of the Indian Constitution. Some important points related to this are, l The Ordinances promulgated by the President have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament [under Article 123(2)]. l The Ordinance is required to get approved by the Parliament, within six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, otherwise it ceases to operate at the expiry of six-weeks from reassembly. l The Ordinance may be withdrawn at any time by the President.

s: Which Article fixes the maximum gap of six months between two sessions of Parliament?
x: Article 85 sets the six-month limit for Parliament; Article 174 does the same for State Legislatures.

s: If the two Houses reassemble on different dates, from which date is the six-week life of an ordinance counted?
o: the earlier of the two dates
the date the Rajya Sabha reassembles
the later of the two dates
x: An ordinance must be laid before the legislature on reassembly, and if the Houses meet on different dates the six weeks run from the later date.

s: After what period of unexcused absence may an MP's seat be vacated under Article 101(4)?
x: Unexcused absence for 60 days can vacate the seat; prorogation and adjournments of more than four consecutive days are left out of the count.

s: What is the maximum life of an ordinance?
x: The gap between sessions can be six months, and the ordinance lapses six weeks after reassembly.

s:
Consider the following statements about an ordinance issued by the President:
1. It ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved.
2. It ceases earlier if both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: An ordinance lapses six weeks after reassembly, and ends earlier if both Houses disapprove it or it is withdrawn.

s: In which of the following cases does an ordinance end before six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament?
o: When the Supreme Court is in vacation
When both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it
When the Lok Sabha Speaker objects
x: Disapproval by resolutions of both Houses, or withdrawal by the President, ends an ordinance earlier.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987)?
o: Every Ordinance automatically becomes a constitutional amendment
Routine re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution
The President’s satisfaction is never subject to review
An Ordinance must remain in force for at least six months
x: D.C. Wadhwa held that routine re-promulgation without placing the Ordinance before the legislature amounts to a fraud on the Constitution.

s: In which case (2017) did the Supreme Court hold that re-promulgation of an Ordinance may be a fraud on the Constitution?
o: Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
A.K. Roy v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
x: Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held that re-promulgation can be a fraud on the Constitution and that laying the Ordinance before the legislature is mandatory.

s: Which recent development revived the debate on the possible misuse of the ordinance-making power and executive overreach?
o: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026
The Inter-State Water Disputes Amendment Ordinance, 2026
x: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 revived the debate on ordinance misuse and executive overreach.

s: What is the principal criticism of the frequent promulgation of ordinances?
o: They can be issued only during a financial emergency.
They require prior approval from the Supreme Court.
They transfer all legislative powers to the States.
x: Frequent ordinances are criticised because they bypass parliamentary deliberation.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Article 368 – amendment power not available through an ordinance
Article 13(2) – an ordinance abridging Part III rights is void
x: The Krishna Kumar Singh case was decided in 2017; 1987 is the D.C. Wadhwa case, which condemned repeated re-promulgation in Bihar.

s: Under which Article did Andhra Pradesh use an ordinance on organ-transplant committees?
x: The Governor's ordinance power is Article 213; AP used it for organ-transplant committees.

src: APPSC Assistant BC Welfare Officer, Royalty Inspector 2020
s: Which Article of the Indian Constitution says that the President shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remission of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence?
Which Article of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to pardon the sentence of a convicted person?
Which of the following Article of the Indian Constitution deals with Pardoning power of the Indian President:
x: Article-72 Article 72 of the Constitution deals with the pardoning power of the President of India. Under this article, the President can grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment, including in death sentence cases. This power is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

s: Power of the President to grant pardons etc. is a :-
x: Under Article 72, the President has the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence. This comes under the judicial power of the President.

s: Under which pardoning power of the President, one form of punishment is substituted by a lighter form?
x: Commutation substitutes a lighter form of punishment (e.g. death to rigorous life imprisonment). Remission only reduces the period.

s: Under which pardoning power of the President, duration of sentence is reduced without changing its character?
x: Remission reduces the duration of the sentence while keeping its character (2 years RI to 1 year RI). Commutation changes the form of punishment.

s: What is the nature of the pardoning power of the President under Article 72?
o: An executive power exercised in his discretion
A judicial power exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice
A legislative power of the Executive
A power exercised on the Supreme Court's advice
x: Article 72 is a judicial power of the President, exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice.

s: Which form of pardoning power reduces a sentence of two years' rigorous imprisonment to one year's rigorous imprisonment?
x: Remission shortens the period without changing the character; commutation changes the form.

s: Which form of pardoning power substitutes a lighter form of punishment?
x: Commutation changes the form (death to rigorous life imprisonment); remission only reduces the period.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Pardon – Removes both sentence and conviction
x: Respite is a lesser sentence for special reasons like pregnancy or disability; a temporary stay of execution is a reprieve.

s:
Consider the following statements about the pardoning power under Article 72:
1. Article 72 covers sentences by court-martial.
2. Amnesty falls within Article 72.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only 1 is correct: Article 72 covers court-martial, Union-law offences and death sentences; amnesty is outside it.

s:
Consider the following statements with regard to pardoning power of the President of India :
I. The exercise of this power by the President can be subjected to limited judicial review.
II. The President can exercise this power without the advice of the Central Government.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Supreme Court has clarified in several judgments that the President’s clemency power is subject to limited judicial review. Therefore, Statement I is correct. Even with respect to the clemency power under Article 72, the President cannot take any executive decision without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. Therefore, Statement II is incorrect.

s: Power to grant pardons are enjoyed by which of the following constitutional authorities?
o: Chief Justice of Supreme Court of India
x: The President (Art. 72) and the Governor (Art. 161) both have pardoning powers, though the Governor's are narrower, as he cannot pardon a death sentence.

s: Which one of the following Statements about the State Governors is not true?
o: He is a part of the State Legislature
He can pardon a sentence of death
He does not appoint Judges of the State High Court
x: According to Article 161, the Governor shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence against any law, but the Governor is not empowered to pardon a sentence of death. All the given statements except statement (b) are accurate.

s: Which Article provides for the Governor's pardoning power?
x: Article 161 gives the Governor pardoning power for offences against State laws.

s: In respect of a death sentence, which of the following can the Governor NOT do?
x: The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence but can suspend, remit or commute it; only the President can pardon it.

s: In which case was limited judicial review of pardons on mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant grounds laid down?
o: Epuru Sudhakar v Govt of AP (2006)
x: Epuru Sudhakar (2006), an AP case, allows limited judicial review of pardons.

s: How did the Supreme Court in Maru Ram (1980) hold that the pardoning power is exercised?
o: On the Council of Ministers' advice
On the advice of the Supreme Court
On the advice of the Home Secretary
x: Maru Ram held the power is exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice.

s: How can the veto of the President of the United States be overridden?
x: The US President has a qualified veto, which Congress can override by a two-thirds majority.

s: Which veto does the Indian President have but the US President does not?
x: India has an absolute veto, which the USA lacks; the USA has a qualified veto, which India lacks.

s: Which of the following Indian Presidents did not grant assent to the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill?
The President of India who for the first time since Independence used the President's power to return a Bill to the Parliament - The Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, was
Which Constitutional Amendment made the President’s satisfaction in promulgating an Ordinance final, and which Amendment reversed that position?
o: 38th Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
39th Amendment made it final; 42nd Amendment reversed it
42nd Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
44th Amendment made it final; 38th Amendment reversed it
x: The 38th Amendment of 1975 made the President’s satisfaction final, while the 44th Amendment reversed that position.
